cards.b: Vietnam shows the strongest case for communism as a vehicle of national liberation. Ho Chi Minh defeated France and, after him, the United States. It also shows the costs: war deaths in the millions, re-education camps and a one-party state still in power.

France conquered Vietnam in the 19th century and ruled it as part of Indochina until 1954. Ho (born Nguyen Sinh Cung, 1890) left in 1911 as a ship's cook, lived in Paris, joined the French Communist Party at the Tours Congress in 1920, studied in Moscow, and founded the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930. He proclaimed independence on 2 September 1945.

In Paris Ho reported on colonialism and wrote Le Procès de la colonisation française (1925). After reading Lenin's "Theses on the National and Colonial Questions" (1920), he said it was this that made him a communist: it promised liberation for his people. The Viet Minh (1941) united all patriots under a nationalist banner, with land reform and anti-Japanese resistance. Marxism was an instrument of independence.

General Vo Nguyen Giap built the army. The Viet Minh defeated the French at Dien Bien Phu (May 1954); at Geneva Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel, with elections promised for 1956 but never held. In the North, Ho's government carried out land reform (1953-56) in which thousands were executed (estimates range from several thousand to tens of thousands) and the leadership later apologised for errors.

South Vietnam under Ngo Dinh Diem was backed by the US. The National Liberation Front (Viet Cong) rose in 1960. Direct US intervention began in 1965 (after the Gulf of Tonkin incident, 1964). Ho died on 2 September 1969. The Tet Offensive (1968) shook American opinion; the Paris Accords (January 1973) led to US withdrawal. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. Total Vietnamese deaths in the wars 1955-75 are commonly estimated at 1.5 to 3.5 million, and some 58,000 Americans died.

Reunified Vietnam (1976) imposed collectivisation in the South, sent hundreds of thousands to "re-education" camps, and had about 800,000 or more "boat people" escape. Its 1978 invasion of Cambodia ended the Khmer Rouge; China attacked in 1979. Facing shortages, the Party launched Doi Moi (renovation) in 1986: markets, private firms and foreign investment, with Party control. Vietnam's GDP has grown 6-7% a year; it is now a manufacturing hub.

Admirers (Frances FitzGerald, Ho's own anti-colonial record) see a patriot. Critics: executions and land-reform terror; the ban on opposition; the repression of dissidents (e.g. the Nhan Van-Giai Pham affair, 1956-58); and the "re-education" camps. Historians (Fredrik Logevall, Embers of War, 2012) note missed chances for compromise in 1946-47. Realists: the US misread a nationalist movement as a Soviet proxy and fought a war it could not win. Marxists doubt that Doi Moi is socialism.

India recognised the Democratic Republic only in 1972, but Nehru and the Left had backed Vietnam's independence; India chaired the International Control Commission after 1954. The slogan "Hanoi, Saigon" marches of the 1960s and the CPI(M)'s activism show a deep solidarity. Today India and Vietnam have a "Comprehensive Strategic Partnership" (2016), partly around the South China Sea. Vietnam's Doi Moi is studied in India's debates on a reform path while preserving the state's role.

Key takeaways

  1. Ho became a communist through Lenin's anti-colonial theses.
  2. The Viet Minh united nationalists; Dien Bien Phu (1954) ended French rule in the north.
  3. The American war (1965-73) ended with the fall of Saigon (1975).
  4. Post-1975: re-education camps, boat people, then Doi Moi (1986).
  5. Debate: nationalist hero or Leninist autocrat.

Debate questions

  1. Was Vietnam's communism more nationalism than Marxism?
  2. Does Doi Moi mean the end of socialism?
